nodes.label: JEGHERS et al. (1949) described a syndrome of generalized intestinal polyposis with melanin spots of the oral mucosa, lips and digits. They considered it to be of diagnostic significance.
BRUWER et al. (1954) used the designation Peutz-Jeghers syndrome for the association of surface pigmentation with generalized intestinal polyposis.
DORMANDY (1957) used the name Peutz-Jeghers syndrome for the combination of gastrointestinal polyposis and mucocutaneous pigmentation.
BARTHOLOMEW et al. (1962) reported on intestinal polyposis associated with mucocutaneous pigmentation.
SHEWARD (1962) reported Peutz-Jeghers syndrome in childhood with unusual radiological features.
KEEN and MURRAY (1962) reported a further family with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
MICHALANY and FERRAZ (1962) reported Peutz syndrome in a family described as mulatto, focusing on the histologic structure of the intestinal polyps.
FARMER et al. (1963) reported 3 cases illustrating the spectrum of the Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
CHRISTIAN et al. (1964) reported Peutz-Jeghers syndrome associated with a functioning ovarian tumor.
WILLIAMS and KNUDSEN (1965) reported Peutz-Jeghers syndrome together with a duodenal carcinoma that had metastasized.
McAllister et al. (1967) reported 17 patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome in 4 generations.

Kieselstein et al. (1969) described a family of Iraqi Jews with mucocutaneous pigmentation and intestinal polyposis (Peutz-Jeghers syndrome) in which polycystic kidney disease also occurred. They also performed a chromosome study.
Scully (1970) described sex cord tumor with annular tubules as a distinctive ovarian tumor of the Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
Sommerhaug and Mason (1970) reported Peutz-Jeghers syndrome occurring together with ureteral polyposis.
McKittrick et al. (1971) reported 2 cases of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, one of which had been followed for 30 years.
Dodds et al. (1972) reported on gastrointestinal malignancy in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. No further details are available from the title alone.
Brigg et al. (1976) reported unusual manifestations of the Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

McAllister and Richards (1977) reported 20 patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome spanning 5 generations, which they described as the largest personal series in the literature. They presented pedigree charts and discussed how the lip spots and intestinal polyps develop and relate to each other.

McAllister and Richards (1977) presented a previously unreported case of colon intussusception in a patient with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. They also discussed how the syndrome presents clinically and its malignant potential.

Lin et al. (1977) reported a patient with Peutz-Jeghers polyposis who had duodenal carcinoma that spread to other sites (metastasizing). The patient did not have the skin pigmentation typical of the syndrome. The patient also had vitiligo, which the authors considered coincidental.

Lin et al. (1977) stated that duodenal carcinoma is the neoplasm most often associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. They reviewed 14 reported cases of the syndrome with intestinal carcinoma. In only 2 of these was the tumor shown to arise in a polyp. The authors believed that the carcinoma in their own patient also developed independently of the polyps.

Babin et al. (1978) reported a patient with oral hyperpigmentation in response to an occult malignancy. They noted that melanocytes in the oral and laryngeal mucosa can respond to occult malignancy with hyperpigmentation, and they discussed how to tell this from other disease processes.

Cochet et al. (1979) described a 56-year-old woman with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and her 29-year-old son, also affected, who both developed metastasising gastrointestinal carcinoma. The mother died of duodenal carcinoma and the son died of gastric carcinoma. In both, the carcinoma developed in hamartomatous polyps and had metastasized extensively.

Cochet et al. (1979) found dysplastic areas within the hamartomatous polyps of both patients. The authors concluded that hamartomatous polyps may, in some cases, be the precursors of digestive tract carcinomas, which supports the malignant potential of Peutz-Jeghers polyps.
Cochet et al. (1979) stated that patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome have a slight, though definite, increased risk of gastrointestinal carcinoma.

Joishy et al. (1979) reported a patient from Malaysia with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, which they described as the first case reported from that country. The patient had repeated (successive) intussusceptions that required extensive small bowel resection.

Matuchansky et al. (1979) described a patient with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome who had an intestinal adenocarcinoma that had spread to the omentum and the celiac lymph nodes. Histology showed that the cancer arose in a jejunal hamartoma. The adenocarcinoma was closely intermixed with smooth muscle bands, and several glands of the polyp showed a clear transitional zone of malignant cells. Near the malignant areas, the polyp's glands had less-differentiated epithelium but were still mixed with nonstriated muscle bundles. The authors took this as strong evidence that the hamartomatous structures had dedifferentiated.

Cantú et al. (1980) described a 6-year-old boy with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and a unilateral feminizing Sertoli cell tumor. Histopathologic study of the nontumorous testicular tissue showed changes in the seminiferous tubules. The authors suggested these changes meant that estrogens, directly or indirectly, may have had both stimulating and atrophying effects. They concluded that gonadal tumors are an additional manifestation of the Peutz-Jeghers syndrome gene in both male and female patients.

In the boy with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and a feminizing Sertoli cell tumor, Cantú et al. (1980) found consistently high estrogen levels in plasma and urine. Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone levels were normal. Estrogen levels did not change in a way that correlated with administration of exogenous gonadotropin, which the authors took as a sign that estrogen production was autonomous.

Riley and Swift (1980) described a family in which the proband and her paternal grandmother both had Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and bilateral breast carcinoma. The proband's breast cancer was premenopausal. When she underwent oophorectomy to treat it, an ovarian sex cord tumor with annular tubules was found incidentally.

Riley and Swift (1980) noted that breast cancer had been reported in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome patients before. They suggested that the Peutz-Jeghers gene may be associated with an increased risk of breast tumors.
Griffith and Bisset (1980) reported 3 cases of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome presenting in early childhood and considered the need for surgical intervention.
Yamada et al. (1981) carried out ultrastructural studies of the pigmented macules of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

Péloquin et al. (1981) reported a 49-year-old woman with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome whose first symptom was deep thrombophlebitis of the leg, which appeared to be part of a paraneoplastic syndrome. She had an adenocarcinoma that arose in a hamartoma of the terminal ileum, with metastases to the ovary and lymph nodes. Later she developed metastases in the cervical lymph nodes, which responded to chemotherapy for a time.

After reviewing the literature on metastatic Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, Péloquin et al. (1981) concluded that metastatic disease is uncommon, but that all patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome should have close long-term follow-up.

Burdick and Prior (1982) followed a family group of 10 patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome for 27 years; 8 family members had 1 or more manifestations of the syndrome. One member died after a bypass procedure for a nonresectable jejunal carcinoma. Postmortem examination showed an adenocarcinoma of the jejunum arising in a Peutz-Jeghers polyp, with metastases in the mesenteric lymph nodes.

In the family reported by Burdick and Prior (1982), 2 members developed breast carcinoma, 1 of which arose in a fibroadenoma. Both patients died: 1 of metastatic breast carcinoma and the other of a second primary malignancy, an adenocarcinoma of the jejunum arising in a Peutz-Jeghers polyp. In addition, 3 family members had benign ovarian tumors, 1 had a benign breast tumor, and 1 had a benign colloid thyroid nodule.

Burdick and Prior (1982) concluded that the exact risk of intestinal cancer in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is unknown but probably very small. They recommended that gastrointestinal surgery continue to be performed in symptomatic patients and that all patients be followed closely at regular intervals.
Solh et al. (1983) reported Peutz-Jeghers syndrome associated with precocious puberty.

DiLiberti et al. (1983) reported a 7.5-year-old boy with macrocephaly, hamartomatous intestinal polyps, and café-au-lait spots on the penis. They regarded this triad as a new disorder, the Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome, distinct from Sotos syndrome. The authors also considered prominent Schwalbe lines, prominent corneal nerves, and lipid storage myopathy to be part of the syndrome.

DiLiberti et al. (1983) suggested autosomal dominant inheritance of Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome because the proband's mother had macrocephaly, a similar facial appearance, and a hamartomatous polyp.
Parker and Knight (1983) reported Peutz-Jeghers syndrome causing obstructive jaundice due to a polyp in the common bile duct.

Lehur et al. (1984) reported a woman with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome who developed bilateral breast carcinoma and then malignant transformation of a duodenal hamartomatous polyp. She died of the duodenal malignancy.

Tweedie and McCann (1984) described a 39-year-old man with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome who developed a caecal adenocarcinoma that had metastasized widely to regional lymph nodes. The carcinoma was accompanied by several other colonic Peutz-Jeghers polyps that showed no dysplasia or malignancy, and it could not be determined whether the carcinoma had arisen from a Peutz-Jeghers polyp. The patient also had gastric and small intestinal polyps.

Tweedie and McCann (1984) found that serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was normal at presentation in their patient with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and metastatic colonic adenocarcinoma, as in one other reported case, and concluded that their report did not support the use of CEA as a screening test in such high-risk groups. They noted that the cancer risk in PJS was unknown and proposed a UK national registry of PJS patients to determine it.

Wilson et al. (1986) described a 6-year-old boy with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, gynecomastia, and multifocal, bilateral testicular tumors. Citing this case and earlier reports, the authors suggested that males with PJS, like females, are at risk of developing gonadal tumors.

Banse-Kupin and Douglass (1986) reported a patient with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome in whom the characteristic pigmented macules developed within preexisting psoriatic plaques, at sites extremely unusual for the syndrome. The authors believed this was the first such case reported in the English literature.

Bowlby (1986) reported a 16-year-old male with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome who had carcinoma of the pancreas. To the author's knowledge, this was the first reported case of pancreatic carcinoma in association with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

Giardiello et al. (1987) followed 31 patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome from 1973 to 1985. Cancer, confirmed by histopathologic review, developed in 15 of the 31 (48%): 4 had gastrointestinal carcinomas, 10 had nongastrointestinal carcinomas and 1 had multiple myeloma. Three other patients developed adenomatous polyps of the stomach and colon.

Giardiello et al. (1987) found that the cancers were diagnosed when patients were relatively young but after Peutz-Jeghers syndrome had been diagnosed; the interval between the two diagnoses was 25 +/- 20 years (range, 1 to 64). By relative-risk analysis, cancer developed 18 times more often than expected in the general population (P less than 0.0001). The authors suggested that patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome have an increased risk of cancer at both gastrointestinal and nongastrointestinal sites.

Giardiello et al. (1987) described Peutz-Jeghers syndrome as an autosomal dominant hereditary disease characterized by hamartomatous polyps of the gastrointestinal tract and mucocutaneous melanin deposits.

Foley et al. (1988) reported 49 years of follow-up of the 'Harrisburg family,' one of the original Peutz-Jeghers families reported by Jeghers. Its 12 affected members made it the largest Peutz-Jeghers kindred reported. Ten patients underwent a total of 75 polypectomies, 1 patient developed short bowel syndrome, and 3 patients died in young adulthood. The authors concluded that Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is not a benign disease.

Foley et al. (1988) found that 2 of the 12 affected members of the Harrisburg family developed gastrointestinal malignancy. One of them had a duodenal carcinoma arising in a hamartoma with adenomatous changes, a progression in the duodenum that had not been reported before. The authors suggested that Peutz-Jeghers syndrome may be a premalignant condition.

Foley et al. (1988) recommended endoscopic removal of gastric, duodenal, and colonic polyps even when they cause no symptoms. When surgery is needed, they suggested intraoperative endoscopy with polypectomy to help prevent short bowel syndrome. They also proposed that colonoscopic screening of patients and their family members may be beneficial and that surveillance for extraintestinal malignancy appeared to be warranted.

Spigelman et al. (1989) reported that malignant tumors developed in 16 (22%) of 72 patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, and all but 1 of these 16 patients died. Nine of the tumors were gastrointestinal and 7 were nongastrointestinal. The relative risk of death was 13 (95% CI 2.7-38.1) from gastrointestinal cancer and 9 (95% CI 4.2-17.3) from all cancers. The chance of dying of cancer by age 57 years was 48%.

Spigelman et al. (1989) reported evidence for a hamartoma-carcinoma sequence in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. They suggested that the gene locus involved is relevant to the development of malignancy in general.

Gass and Glatzer (1991) described a 74-year-old man with an occult carcinoma of the colon. He developed pigmentation of the mouth and penis typical of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, and this was the first manifestation of bilateral diffuse uveal melanocytic proliferation. The authors suggested that bilateral diffuse uveal melanocytic proliferation may be caused by activation of occult melanocytic naevus cells in response to a hormone-producing carcinoma or to some other common oncogenic stimulus.

Veraldi et al. (1991) described 4 adults with Laugier-Hunziker syndrome, a disorder in the differential diagnosis of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. The patients were 2 men and 2 women aged 39 to 57 years, and all had pigmentation of the lower lip and hard palate. Two patients also had pigmentation of the buccal mucosa. Another patient also had pigmentation of the upper lip, gums, soft palate and the fingers of both hands.

In the 4 patients with Laugier-Hunziker syndrome, Veraldi et al. (1991) found on histology that melanin had accumulated in the basal-layer keratinocytes and that melanophages were increased in the papillary dermis. Electron microscopy showed many mature melanosomes in the basal keratinocytes and in the melanophages. The melanocytes showed no alterations.
Coen et al. (1991) reported an aromatase-producing sex-cord tumor that caused gynecomastia before puberty.

Eng et al. (1991) described a 67-year-old white man with esophageal adenocarcinoma who presented with Peutz-Jeghers-like melanotic macules on the lips, face, nipples, and rectal mucosa. Pathologic examination of the macules showed atypical, pleomorphic large melanocytes in the epidermis that resembled the neoplastic cells of melanoma in situ. The authors stated that this was the first report of atypical melanocyte proliferation in Peutz-Jeghers-like melanosis associated with primary esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Fernandez Seara et al. (1995) reported a 15-day-old girl with generalized gastrointestinal polyposis resulting from Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Her manifestations included abdominal distention, hematemesis, bloody diarrhea, and edema. She died at 1 year of age of multiple complications of her disease.

Young et al. (1995) described 2 young boys with probable Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and multicentric Sertoli cell testicular tumors. Both boys had prominent gynecomastia, rapid growth, advanced bone age, and markedly elevated serum estradiol. Serum anti-mullerian hormone, measured in 1 boy, was in the normal range for age. Bilateral orchiectomy was performed in both because the tumor growth would likely cause sterility and continued high estradiol threatened their adult height potential. Four similar cases in boys with PJS had been reported before.

Under the microscope, the testicular tumors described by Young et al. (1995) consisted of greatly enlarged seminiferous tubules packed with ovoid Sertoli-like cells. A prominent eosinophilic basement membrane surrounded the tubules and extended between the cells, forming hyalinized ovoid globules and microcalcifications. Electron microscopy showed layered basement membranes around adjacent cells and ovoid cells with abundant cytoplasm and limited smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

Young et al. (1995) found increased transcription of the aromatase cytochrome P450 gene in testicular tumor tissue from both boys with PJS. Transcription used promoter II, the promoter that drives aromatase expression in the normal ovary and testis. Transcript levels were similar to those in corpus luteum, resulting in increased estrogen synthesis. Transcripts from the placental-type aromatase promoters I.1 and I.2 were not detected at significant levels.

Markie et al. (1996) found a pericentric inversion of chromosome 6 on karyotype analysis of a patient with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. They used FISH with YAC clones containing chromosome 6 genetic markers and a centromeric alphoid repeat probe. One inversion breakpoint lay within the alphoid array, in a 1-cM interval between D6S257 and D6S402. The other lay in a 4-cM interval between D6S403 and D6S311. The oestrogen receptor gene locus (ESR) was excluded from the second interval.

Hemminki et al. (1997) used comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) of Peutz-Jeghers polyps, together with loss of heterozygosity (LOH) studies, to search for a putative tumor suppressor locus. Linkage analysis in 12 families, using markers from the deletion site, showed a high-penetrance locus in distal 19p. The multipoint lod score was 7.00 at marker D19S886.
In their linkage analysis of 12 Peutz-Jeghers families, Hemminki et al. (1997) found no evidence of genetic heterogeneity for the distal 19p locus.

Hemminki et al. (1997) concluded that their CGH and LOH findings in Peutz-Jeghers polyps pointed to a putative tumor suppressor locus. They also concluded that the findings gave molecular evidence that hamartomas have malignant potential.

Hemminki et al. (1997) described Peutz-Jeghers syndrome as a condition with intestinal hamartomatous polyposis and melanin spots on the lips, buccal mucosa and digits. They noted that a greatly elevated risk of malignancy had been documented, and that gastrointestinal tumors and cancers of the breast, ovary, testis and uterine cervix appear to be overrepresented.

Amos et al. (1997) confirmed linkage of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome to the telomeric region of chromosome 19p and refined the localization of the locus. In the 5 families they examined, there were no recombinants with marker D19S886. The multipoint lod score at D19S886 was 7.52.
Amos et al. (1997) found no evidence for genetic heterogeneity among the 5 Peutz-Jeghers syndrome families they studied.

In the 5 families, Amos et al. (1997) found that all carriers of the at-risk haplotype expressed the Peutz-Jeghers phenotype and no noncarriers showed Peutz-Jeghers sequelae. They concluded that penetrance was complete and that there were no sporadic cases.

Mehenni et al. (1997) performed a genomewide linkage analysis in 6 PJS families (2 from Spain, 2 from India, 1 from the United States, and 1 from Portugal) comprising 93 individuals, 39 of them affected. Marker D19S886 gave a maximum lod score of 4.74 at theta = 0.045, and multipoint analysis gave a lod score of 7.51 for the interval between D19S886 and 19pter, confirming a PJS locus on 19p13.3.

Mehenni et al. (1997) found that markers on 19q13.4 also showed significant evidence for linkage in PJS families (maximum lod score of 3.8 at theta = 0.13 for D19S880), mostly contributed by a single family, PJS07. They suggested that a potential second PJS locus on 19q13.4 exists in a minority of families.

Mehenni et al. (1997) described Peutz-Jeghers syndrome as an autosomal dominant disorder with variable expression and incomplete penetrance, characterized by mucocutaneous pigmentation and hamartomatous polyposis, with an increased frequency of gastrointestinal and extraintestinal malignancies (ovaries, testes, and breast).

Jenne et al. (1998) identified a novel human gene encoding the serine threonine kinase STK11, 190 kb proximal to marker D19S886 in the Peutz-Jeghers syndrome linkage region on 19p13.3. In a 3-generation PJS family, they found an STK11 allele with a deletion of exons 4 and 5 and an inversion of exons 6 and 7 that segregated with the disease.

nodes.label: By sequence analysis of STK11 exons in 4 unrelated PJS patients, Jenne et al. (1998) identified 3 nonsense mutations and 1 acceptor splice site mutation. All 5 germline mutations found in the study were predicted to disrupt the function of the kinase domain. The authors concluded that germline STK11 mutations, probably in conjunction with acquired defects of the second allele in somatic cells, cause PJS.

Jenne et al. (1998) described Peutz-Jeghers syndrome as an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by melanocytic macules of the lips, multiple gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps, and an increased risk for various neoplasms, including gastrointestinal cancer.

Hemminki et al. (1998) found truncating germline mutations in LKB1, a gene on chromosome 19p, in multiple individuals with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. They concluded that PJS was the first cancer-susceptibility syndrome found to be caused by inactivating mutations in a protein kinase.
Hemminki et al. (1998) described Peutz-Jeghers syndrome as a rare hereditary disease that predisposes to benign and malignant tumors in many organ systems.

Hemminki et al. (1998) reported that LKB1, a gene that had already been identified but not mapped, is strongly homologous to XEEK1, a cytoplasmic serine/threonine protein kinase from Xenopus, and more weakly similar to many other protein kinases.

Olschwang et al. (1998) analyzed 20 further families with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, beyond the 12 families previously found to be compatible with linkage to marker D19S886, and found that most were consistent with a PJS gene on 19p13.3. They concluded that chromosome 19p13.3 holds a major PJS locus.

Olschwang et al. (1998) found that 3 of 20 Peutz-Jeghers syndrome families were unlinked to 19p13.3, and none of the available PJS polyps from these families showed allele loss at D19S886. The linked and unlinked families showed no obvious clinicopathologic or ethnic differences. The authors suggested that there may be a minor PJS locus (or loci) elsewhere in the genome.

Kato et al. (1998) used ruby laser therapy to treat labial lentigines in 2 children with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. The response was excellent, and the lesions did not recur and left no sequelae. The authors suggested that ruby laser therapy is safe and suitable for treating labial lentigines in children with PJS.

Mehenni et al. (1998) screened 9 PJS families of American, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Turkish, and Indian origin for LKB1 mutations and found 7 novel mutations: 2 frameshift mutations, 1 four-amino-acid deletion, 2 amino acid substitutions, and 2 splicing errors.

Mehenni et al. (1998) expressed the mutant LKB1 proteins K78I, D176N, W308C, and L67P. All 4 mutants had lost autophosphorylation (kinase) activity. The authors concluded that loss of LKB1 kinase activity is probably responsible for the PJS phenotypes.

Mehenni et al. (1998) found no LKB1 mutation in 2 Indian PJS families. They had previously found linkage to markers on 19q13.3-q13.4 in one of these families, which suggested locus heterogeneity in PJS.

Mehenni et al. (1998) described PJS as an autosomal dominant disease with mucocutaneous pigmentation and hamartomatous polyps, and with an increased risk of benign and malignant tumors in the gastrointestinal tract and in tissues outside it.

Gruber et al. (1998) studied 6 PJS families from the Johns Hopkins Polyposis Registry, including the family originally described by Jeghers in 1949. Linkage analysis confirmed linkage to 19p13.3, near the STK11 gene.
Gruber et al. (1998) sequenced genomic DNA and identified germline STK11 mutations in all 6 PJS families studied, including the original Jeghers family.

In hamartomas and adenocarcinomas from PJS patients, Gruber et al. (1998) found loss of heterozygosity (LOH) of 19p markers near STK11 in 70% of tumors. Haplotype analysis showed that the retained allele carried the germline mutation, which the authors said confirmed that STK11 is a tumor suppressor gene. They concluded that STK11 acts as an early gatekeeper regulating hamartoma development and suggested that hamartomas may be precursors of adenocarcinoma.

Gruber et al. (1998) found LOH of 17p and 18q in an adenocarcinoma but not in hamartomas, which they took to mean these are late events in PJS cancer progression. The adenocarcinomas with 17p LOH also showed altered p53 on immunohistochemistry. None of the 18 PJS tumors showed microsatellite instability, LOH on 5q near APC, or mutations in K-ras codons 12 or 13.

Westerman et al. (1999) reported a follow-up of more than 78 years of the original Dutch family described by Peutz in 1921. They studied the natural history of PJS across 6 generations using interviews, physical examination, chart review and histologic review. Clinical features included gastrointestinal polyposis, mucocutaneous pigmentation, nasal polyposis and rectal extrusion of polyps. Intestinal obstruction and the development of malignant disease reduced the survival of affected family members, and the authors suggested that PJS is not a benign disease.

In the original Dutch PJS family first described by Peutz, Westerman et al. (1999) identified a novel germline mutation in the LKB1 gene that cosegregated with the disease. The mutation was a T insertion at codon 66 in exon 1, which caused a frameshift and a stop at codon 162 in exon 4. The authors concluded that an inactivating germline LKB1 mutation is involved in the PJS phenotype in this, the oldest known affected kindred.

nodes.label: Westerman et al. (1999) noted that Peutz first recognized the association of heredity, gastrointestinal polyposis and mucocutaneous pigmentation in a Dutch family in 1921.

Westerman et al. (1999) performed mutation analysis of LKB1/STK11 in 19 predominantly Dutch PJS families and identified 12 novel mutations in 12 families: 1 nonsense mutation, 3 frameshift deletions, 3 frameshift insertions, 2 acceptor splice site mutations, and 3 missense mutations. None of the mutations occurred in more than one family, and a number were shown to have arisen de novo. Four polymorphisms were also detected.
Westerman et al. (1999) found no apparent abnormalities of the LKB1/STK11 gene in 7 of 19 PJS families, which they suggested could reflect locus heterogeneity in PJS.

Westerman et al. (1999) noted that the diverse array of mutations, apparent high mutation rate, and possible second PJS locus make diagnostic or predictive genetic testing in individual patients difficult.

In a review, Westerman and Wilson (1999) noted that the risks from polyps in PJS patients include surgical emergencies such as small bowel intussusception, and chronic or acute bleeding from the polyps.

Westerman and Wilson (1999) reviewed reports suggesting that PJS is associated with both gastrointestinal and non-gastrointestinal tumours. It was not clear whether these cancers arise from the polyps. The authors suggested that the frequent occurrence of rare extraintestinal cancers points to a general susceptibility to cancer. These include sex cord tumours with annular tubules of the ovary, adenoma malignum of the cervix, and Sertoli cell tumours of the testis.

Westerman and Wilson (1999) noted that the PJS gene had recently been identified as encoding the serine threonine kinase STK11. Because of the general susceptibility to cancer in PJS, they stated that the gene is thought to act as a tumour suppressor.

Westerman and Wilson (1999) concluded that people who carry the PJS gene are at increased risk of cancer both inside and outside the gastrointestinal tract. As genetic identification of carriers without symptoms becomes possible, they said surveillance and screening protocols need to be developed for patients and their relatives.

Jiang et al. (1999) screened 10 unrelated families with PJS for germline STK11 changes, using the protein truncation test and genomic DNA sequencing. They found a novel truncating deletion covering STK11 exons 2 through 7 in a single patient, as well as several known polymorphisms.
STK11 truncating deletion spanning STK11 exons 2-7

Jiang et al. (1999) studied loss of heterozygosity in PJS polyps from 4 patients and found an allelic deletion of D19S886 in a patient other than the one carrying the STK11 deletion. Because germline STK11 mutations were found in only 1 of 10 families, the authors suggested that STK11 mutations account for only a proportion of PJS cases.
Bergadá et al. (2000) described a prepubertal boy with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, gynecomastia, and bilateral neoplastic Sertoli cell proliferation.

In the prepubertal boy with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, gynecomastia, and bilateral Sertoli cell proliferation, Bergadá et al. (2000) found that the only abnormal hormonal finding was increased serum concentrations of inhibin B and Pro-alpha C. They noted that gynecomastia in boys with PJS and Sertoli cell tumors results from increased estrogen production due to increased aromatase activity within the testicular tumor.

Boardman et al. (2000) screened LKB1 for mutations in 5 PJS kindreds with more than 2 affected members, 5 probands with only 1 other affected relative, and 23 individuals with sporadic PJS, using conformation-sensitive gel electrophoresis, direct sequencing, and long-range PCR for larger insertions or deletions. LKB1 mutations were found in only 2 probands with a family history of PJS and in 4 of 23 sporadic cases. The authors suggested significant genetic heterogeneity for PJS and the involvement of other loci.
Boardman et al. (2000) found LKB1 mutations in 6 of 33 PJS probands studied: 2 of 10 probands with a family history of PJS and 4 of 23 individuals with sporadic PJS.

Miyaki et al. (2000) studied 27 gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps from 10 patients in 9 PJS families and found germline LKB1 mutations in 6 families. Somatic LKB1 mutations were found in 5 polyps, and loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at the LKB1 locus on 19p was seen in 14 other polyps.

Miyaki et al. (2000) suggested that gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps in PJS develop through inactivation of LKB1 by a germline mutation plus somatic mutation or LOH of the unaffected allele. Additional mutations of beta-catenin and p53 were suggested to convert hamartomatous polyps into adenomatous and carcinomatous lesions. Adenomatous lesions microdissected from hamartomatous polyps had both a beta-catenin mutation and 19p LOH. A carcinomatous lesion in a gastric hamartomatous polyp had a p53 mutation and LOH at the p53 locus in addition to LKB1 LOH and a beta-catenin mutation. K-ras mutations were found in a few polyps, but no APC mutations or 5q LOH were found.

Entius et al. (2001) analyzed 39 polyps and 5 carcinomas from 17 patients from 13 families with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome for loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at 19p13.3 (the STK11/LKB1 locus). LOH at 19p was found in 15 of the 39 polyps and in all 5 carcinomas; 6 of 7 polyps from patients with cancer had LOH compared with 9 of 31 polyps from the other patients (p = 0.01). The authors concluded that STK11/LKB1 acts as a tumor suppressor gene and may be involved in the early stages of PJS tumorigenesis, and that further research was needed to see whether LOH in PJS polyps could be used as a biomarker to predict cancer.
Entius et al. (2001) found that a polyp from a PJS patient without a germline STK11/LKB1 mutation showed no LOH at 19p or at 3 alternative PJS candidate loci (19q, 6p, and 6q).

Entius et al. (2001) found no LOH at 5q (APC) in PJS polyps or carcinomas, but APC mutations were found in 4 of 5 carcinomas. No 17p LOH was seen and no p53 mutation was found, although p53 immunostaining was present in 1 carcinoma and focally in 3 polyps; 1 carcinoma had an activating K-ras codon 12 mutation and another showed 18q LOH without loss of SMAD4 expression. The authors suggested that differences from the colorectal adenoma-carcinoma sequence indicate a distinct pathway of carcinogenesis in PJS.

Olschwang et al. (2001) analyzed the STK11/LKB1 locus in 34 Peutz-Jeghers syndrome families. They searched the coding sequence for mutations and rearrangements and also used allele-specific expression tests and linkage studies. They found germline deleterious STK11/LKB1 mutations in 70% of cases.

Olschwang et al. (2001) found that their results strengthened the hypothesis of a second PJS locus. PJS families fell into two groups depending on whether an STK11/LKB1 alteration had been identified. The authors concluded that up to 30% of PJS patients have the disorder because of mutation in an unidentified gene.

Olschwang et al. (2001) found that cancer risk differed markedly between PJS families with and without an identified STK11/LKB1 mutation. PJS patients without an identified STK11/LKB1 mutation were at major risk for proximal biliary adenocarcinoma, which is an infrequent tumor in the general population.
Keller et al. (2001) reviewed the history of Jan Peutz and Harold Jeghers, the names behind the eponymous syndrome, which combines polyposis with pigmentation of the skin and mucous membranes.
Keller et al. (2002) reported molecular genetic evidence of an association between nasal polyposis and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

Buchet-Poyau et al. (2002) noted that STK11 mutations cannot be detected in a considerable number of PJS patients, suggesting genetic heterogeneity. They studied PJS07, a family without STK11 mutations in which multipoint linkage analysis had previously given significant LOD scores for a second potential PJS locus on 19q13.3-q13.4, between markers D19S180 and D19S254.

In the PJS07 family, Buchet-Poyau et al. (2002) screened all exons and exon-intron junctions of 4 candidate genes in the 19q13.3-q13.4 region: PSCD2, KLK10, PRKCG, and STK13. They first determined the genomic structure of PSCD2 and PRKCG. No pathogenic mutation was found in affected individuals; the only change was a very rare polymorphism in PSCD2 causing a conserved Lys-to-Arg substitution. The authors concluded that these 4 genes were excluded as candidates for the second PJS locus.

Buchet-Poyau et al. (2002) also excluded the STK11-interacting protein gene STK11IP (LIP1), which maps to 2q36, as a candidate for PJS in the PJS07 family. They noted that it could still be a good candidate in other families without STK11 mutations.
Le Meur et al. (2004) reported a family with typical features of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, including gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps, breast cancers, and melanin spots of the oral mucosa.

In a family with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, Le Meur et al. (2004) used quantitative multiplex PCR of short fluorescent fragments (QMPSF) of the 19p13 region to identify an approximately 250-kb heterozygous germline deletion removing the entire STK11 locus. They stated this was the first description of a complete germline deletion of STK11 and suggested that large genomic deletions should be considered in PJS families without detectable STK11 point mutations.

nodes.label: Le Meur et al. (2004) noted that detection of STK11 germline mutations in only 50 to 70% of PJS families had suggested genetic heterogeneity, but their finding of a complete STK11 deletion indicated that large genomic deletions may account for some mutation-negative families.

Amos et al. (2004) characterized STK11 mutations in 42 independent probands and detected mutations in 22 of 32 (69%) probands with PJS and in none of 10 probands referred to rule out PJS. Real-time PCR quantitation of DNA failed to detect large deletions in PJS participants without STK11 mutations. The authors concluded that direct sequencing of STK11 yields a high rate of point mutations in individuals who meet phenotypic PJS criteria.

In a historical cohort of 51 individuals with PJS who completed self-administered questionnaires, Amos et al. (2004) found a median time to onset of gastrointestinal symptoms or polypectomy of 13 years, with wide variability. Gastric polyps were frequent, with a median age at onset of 16 years; the authors suggested that the common occurrence of gastric polyps may facilitate chemopreventive studies.

Amos et al. (2004) found that individuals with missense mutations in STK11 had a significantly later time to onset of first polypectomy (p = 0.04) and of other symptoms compared with those with truncating mutations or no detectable mutation.
Amos et al. (2004) concluded that STK11 mutation analysis should be restricted to individuals who meet PJS criteria or their close relatives.

Hernan et al. (2004) identified a de novo heterozygous germline mutation in exon 6 of the STK11/LKB1 gene in a simplex case of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. The mutation was described as a substitution of cytosine for guanine at codon 246, resulting in a premature stop codon (Tyr246X). The authors predicted that it would produce a truncated protein with presumed loss of kinase activity. The mutation was not found in either parent.

Hernan et al. (2004) used real-time fluorescence PCR genotyping with fluorescent resonance energy transfer to study loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at the LKB1 locus. They used DNA from microdissected gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps from a PJS patient with a de novo Tyr246X mutation. The results suggested that hamartomatous polyps form by a mechanism other than LOH.
Shinmura et al. (2005) described 2 sibs with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome complicated by primary gastric cancer.

In 2 sibs with PJS and primary gastric cancer, Shinmura et al. (2005) identified a novel germline STK11 mutation, c.890delG, predicted to encode a truncated protein (p.Arg297fsX38), by sequencing. No germline mutations in CDH1 or TP53 were detected. No inactivation of the wildtype STK11 allele by somatic mutation, chromosomal deletion, or 5-prime CpG hypermethylation was detected in the gastric cancer.
Schumacher et al. (2005) studied STK11 genotyping in relation to cancer risk in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Only the title was available, so no specific results could be recorded.

Alhopuro et al. (2008) screened patients with colorectal cancer, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS), and juvenile polyposis for MYH11 mutations, prompted by the zebrafish meltdown (mlt) mutant, which carries a recessive ATPase-activating smooth-muscle myosin mutation and develops intestinal abnormalities reminiscent of PJS and juvenile polyposis. They found a germline protein-elongating frameshift mutation in MYH11 in one individual with PJS.

Alhopuro et al. (2008) functionally evaluated the MYH11 frameshift mutations and found that they resulted in unregulated myosin molecules displaying constitutive motor activity, similar to the mutant myosin underlying the zebrafish mlt phenotype. They suggested that unregulated MYH11 may affect cellular energy balance or disturb cell lineage decisions in tumor progenitor cells, and that MYH11 mutations appear to contribute to human intestinal neoplasia.
